item.title: More than 723,000 voters registered
item.description: Fiji had 723,771 registered voters as of June 30, 2026, with the Central Division accounting for the largest share of the country’s electorate. The latest 2026 National Register of Voters Statistics show the Central Division has 313,135 registered voters, followed by the Western Division with 270,175.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji had 723,771 registered voters as of June 30, 2026, with the Central Division accounting for the largest share of the country’s electorate.

The latest 2026 National Register of Voters Statistics show the Central Division has 313,135 registered voters, followed by the Western Division with 270,175.

The Northern Division recorded 102,304 voters, while the Eastern Division had 25,266.

A further 12,891 voters were registered overseas.

The statistics also show an almost even gender split among registered voters, with 362,438 males and 361,333 females — a difference of just 1,105 voters.

Among male voters, the largest age group is 21 to 30 years, with 73,724 registered voters, followed by those aged 31 to 40 with 64,376.

For females, the 21 to 30 age category is also the largest, accounting for 73,226 voters, while 60,052 are aged between 31 and 40.

The figures show younger voters make up a significant portion of Fiji’s electoral roll, with more than 146,000 men and women registered in the 21-to-30 age bracket.

At the other end of the age spectrum, 15,722 male voters and 8,819 female voters are aged 81 years and above.

The voter statistics provide a snapshot of Fiji’s electorate as preparations continue towards the country’s next general election.

The figures are based on the National Register of Voters as at June 30, 2026.

item.title: 17 child HIV deaths were preventable – Dr Soqo
item.description: SEVENTEEN children under the age of 15 have died from HIV, a figure the Ministry of Health and Medical Services describes as one of the highest in the world. Principal Medical Officer for Sexual and Reproductive Health and HIV Unit Harm Reduction Lead Dr Sailosi Soqo said the deaths were preventable.
item.content:encoded:
SEVENTEEN children under the age of 15 have died from HIV, a figure the Ministry of Health and Medical Services describes as one of the highest in the world.

Principal Medical Officer for Sexual and Reproductive Health and HIV Unit Harm Reduction Lead Dr Sailosi Soqo said the deaths were preventable.

He made the revelation while speaking at the 43rd Fiji Head Teachers Association annual conference in Nadi.

He also raised concern over the number of people presenting late for HIV treatment, saying almost one-third of those who come to health facilities have advanced HIV.

“Almost a third that come to us have advanced HIV, and all those cases of HIV that died in 2025, 90 per cent was diagnosed in 2016.”

Dr Soqo said some people diagnosed with advanced HIV died in the same year they sought treatment, with some dying within a month.

He said the number of babies acquiring HIV from their mothers was also increasing each year, despite mother-to-child transmission being preventable.

Dr Soqo identified injecting drug use as a major driver of HIV transmission, while unsafe sexual intercourse was also a significant factor.

He said 42 per cent of people living with HIV reported injecting drug use as their route of transmission.

Dr Soqo also demonstrated the damage caused to needles through repeated use, comparing a new needle with needles used once, twice and six times.

He said the demonstration highlighted the risks associated with repeated needle use and needle sharing among injecting drug users.

item.title: Sayed-Khaiyum, Sagar trial begins today
item.description: The trial of former Fiji Broadcasting Corporation chief executive officer Riyaz Sayed-Khaiyum and chief financial officer Vimlesh Sagar begins today in the Suva Magistrates Court. Mr Sayed-Khaiyum faces charges of abuse of office for gain and an alternative charge of general dishonesty causing a loss, while Mr Sagar is charged with general dishonesty.
item.content:encoded:
The trial of former Fiji Broadcasting Corporation chief executive officer Riyaz Sayed-Khaiyum and chief financial officer Vimlesh Sagar begins today in the Suva Magistrates Court.

Mr Sayed-Khaiyum faces charges of abuse of office for gain and an alternative charge of general dishonesty causing a loss, while Mr Sagar is charged with general dishonesty.

Mr Sayed-Khaiyum is alleged to have pursued five legal proceedings without the knowledge and approval of the FBC board of directors at a cost of $138,813.37, which were not in the interest of the company. The alleged incidents occurred between July 1, 2017, and January 31, 2023.

Mr Sagar is charged with general dishonesty, having allegedly caused a loss by approving payments to R. Patel Lawyers without the prior approval of the FBC board, amounting to $15,075.88.

The prosecution is expected to call between 10 and 15 witnesses.

Bench warrant issued for accused in barracks break-in case

item.title: Court suspends jail sentence
item.description: A 21-YEAR-OLD man convicted of defiling a 14-year-old girl in Labasa has had his 10-month jail term suspended for two years. Justice Lee James Burney sentenced the man earlier this month for a count of defilement and sexual assault.
item.content:encoded:
A 21-YEAR-OLD man convicted of defiling a 14-year-old girl in Labasa has had his 10-month jail term suspended for two years.

Justice Lee James Burney sentenced the man earlier this month for a count of defilement and sexual assault.

He was also placed under a Community-Based Corrections Order for one year.

The court was told the man was 19 when he began a relationship with the victim, who was then 14.

On April 24, 2025, the victim and her sisters went to the man’s cousin’s house for a sleepover, where the offending occurred.

The matter came to light after the victim’s younger sister reported what she had seen.

The man initially told police the sexual activity was consensual and said he did not know the girl’s age.

However, the pre-sentence report stated he had since accepted responsibility, expressed remorse, and acknowledged that he knew she was under 16.

Justice Burney found his youth and lack of maturity contributed to his poor decision-making, while noting the seriousness of the offending.

The judge said the man’s good prospects of rehabilitation weighed strongly in favour of suspending the sentence.

item.title: You can’t blame NZ PM Luxon or PM Rabuka for crimes – Singh
item.description: Minister for Multi-Ethnic Affairs Charan Jeath Singh has questioned whether Prime Ministers of New Zealand Christopher Luxon and Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka should be blamed for individual crimes occurring in their respective countries, as he responded to concerns about vandalism and damage to places of worship. Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Singh referred to recent break-ins involving t
item.content:encoded:
Minister for Multi-Ethnic Affairs Charan Jeath Singh has questioned whether Prime Ministers of New Zealand Christopher Luxon and Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka should be blamed for individual crimes occurring in their respective countries, as he responded to concerns about vandalism and damage to places of worship.

Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Singh referred to recent break-ins involving two of his friends in Epsom, Auckland, to argue that individual incidents should not automatically be attributed to a government or its leader.

“Last week in New Zealand I had two friends, two friends whose house was broken into, in Epsom,” Mr Singh said.

“Epsom is a high-class area of Auckland. Now, do you then blame Mr Luxon, the Prime Minister, because of what had happened?”

“Do you then blame Honourable Rabuka here?” Mr Singh asked.

Mr Singh went on to criticise the former government, claiming problems facing the country had developed over its 16 years in office.

Speaker Filimone Jitoko subsequently intervened and directed the Minister back to the question.

“You’ve done enough background analysis,” the Speaker said.

Addressing the substantive issue, Mr Singh said his Ministry strongly condemned vandalism, damage or deterioration of any place of worship.

“This Ministry strongly condemns any act of vandalism, damage or deterioration of places of worship, whether it involves Hindu temples, churches, mosques or any other places of religious significance,” he said.

Mr Singh said such acts were contrary to the values of religious tolerance, respect and peaceful coexistence.

He said the Ministry had visited a number of affected sites and engaged directly with communities.

Mr Singh said circumstances differed between incidents, with some appearing isolated while others had raised concerns among affected communities over whether they could have been religiously motivated.

He also noted that many places of worship, particularly temples, were easily accessible to the public and had limited security or caretaker presence outside worship hours.

item.title: Children as young as 10 trapped in drug addiction
item.description: Children as young as 10 to 14 years old are becoming trapped in drug addiction in Fiji, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week. Ms Kiran said decades of exposure to illicit drugs had left families vulnerable, despite efforts by national taskforces to disrupt drug supply chains.
item.content:encoded:
Children as young as 10 to 14 years old are becoming trapped in drug addiction in Fiji, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week.

Ms Kiran said decades of exposure to illicit drugs had left families vulnerable, despite efforts by national taskforces to disrupt drug supply chains.

“Most concerning of all, children as young as 10 years to 14 years of age are now becoming trapped in the cycle of addiction,” she said.

“These figures are not merely statistics — they reflect a profound national challenge that demands coordinated, compassionate and evidence-based intervention.”

Ms Kiran said police records traced the influx of hard drugs to before 2009, with the situation continuing to worsen.

She said Fiji recorded 1501 illicit substance cases in 2020, including 100 involving methamphetamine and four involving cocaine.

“The data paints a sobering picture,” she said.

Ms Kiran said the impact was being seen through rising youth mortality, crime and public health risks, including HIV transmission through shared needles.

She said Fiji had historically lacked an integrated recovery programme specifically designed for adolescents, while a shortage of specialist child psychologists and psychiatrists had also affected treatment outcomes.

“Today, Madam Deputy Speaker, we are actively changing this narrative,” Ms Kiran said.

She said Government, in partnership with Empower Pacific, had established Fiji’s first dedicated residential recovery facility for adolescent boys aged 14 to 17.

The Lautoka facility, named Na Sala Vou — “a new pathway for our boys” — provides a structured environment for young people to recover, learn and rebuild their lives.

“This represents a monumental milestone, Madam Deputy Speaker, and a powerful statement of our belief that every child deserves a second chance, that recovery is possible, and that healing is our collective responsibility,” Ms Kiran said.

item.title: Government talks consultation but fails to deliver – Koya
item.description: Opposition MP Faiyaz Koya has accused the Government of repeatedly preaching “consultation, consultation, consultation” while failing to adequately involve the public before introducing major legislative changes. Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Koya pointed to several pieces of legislation which he claimed demonstrated shortcomings in the consultation process.
item.content:encoded:
Opposition MP Faiyaz Koya has accused the Government of repeatedly preaching “consultation, consultation, consultation” while failing to adequately involve the public before introducing major legislative changes.

Speaking in Parliament last week, Mr Koya pointed to several pieces of legislation which he claimed demonstrated shortcomings in the consultation process.

“They stand here and harp about consultation, consultation, consultation. Yet they do not do it thoroughly,” Mr Koya said.

He cited the Tourism Bill, Crimes Decree and Criminal Records Bill 2025 as examples.

“The Tourism Bill was never thoroughly discussed with the people, the Crimes Decree was never thoroughly discussed with the people,” he said.

“The Criminal Records Bill 2025, we went out as a committee and when we spoke to the people, they said they were not consulted.”

Mr Koya also revisited changes to the Liquor Act, which reduced nightclub operating hours from 5am to 1am on public safety grounds.

He said while concerns about brawls, robberies and public safety were legitimate, the economic consequences for businesses should have been properly considered before the changes were introduced.

“There were businesses that were still recovering from COVID-19, but you shut them down,” Mr Koya said.

He said the Government eventually reversed course on the operating hours and claimed the experience demonstrated why meaningful consultation was important.

Mr Koya also questioned an earlier consultation cited by Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga.

“He even said when he was asked by me, where did you do the consultation? ‘We did the consultation in Levuka somewhere with respect to that’,” Mr Koya said.

Mr Koya said he was not opposed to amending laws but argued consultation should identify potential consequences before legislation was changed.

“The experience should teach the Acting Attorney-General and this Government an important lesson — the purpose of consultation is to identify these consequences before we amend the law,” he said.

“We have no problem in amending the law, but you must look at its purpose properly.”
